title: A landing is one commit per task on main's first-parent line, saying what landed
prompt:
Read, in crates/spawn-cli/src/integrate.rs, `judge_pushed()`, `landing_candidate()`, `commit_landing()`, `land()`, `freshness()` and the module comment; `GATED` in crates/spawn-postgres/src/missions.rs (what the integrator reads of a task); the `task.gated` and `task.landed` cases of `spawn_integrator_record` in crates/spawn-postgres/sql/schema.sql; `brief()` in crates/spawn-cli/src/objectives.rs (a brief's first line is `Objective <id>: <title>`); the report template in crates/spawn-cli/src/deliver.rs (`## Outcome`, `## What changed`, `## Open issues`); `names_files_outside_git` in crates/spawn-host/src/git.rs; docs/storage.md ("Landing"), docs/fleet-architecture.md §10.3, and docs/design.md §10 and §14 (the causality invariant).

The problem. A landing does not say what landed. When the source's main is an ancestor of the worker's pushed head, `landing_candidate` returns the pushed head itself and `land()` fast-forwards main to it, so main's history is the worker's checkpoints, every one titled `spawn checkpoint exec_<n>`. Supply PA's main (12 objectives landed, mirrored to GitHub) reads `spawn checkpoint exec_89` from top to bottom: no commit names a task, an objective or what changed, the landings cannot be told from the checkpoints between them, and a landing cannot be found, reviewed or reverted as a unit. When main moved, the landing is a merge titled `Land task <n> (merged with main)`, which names the task and nothing else. Everything the message needs is already in the record: the task id, its objective (`mission_tasks.objective`) and the objective's title (the brief's first line), and the worker's report (`mission_tasks.report`, the report the gate's verdict is for).

Required behaviour (the contract the gate checks).
1. One commit per landing, on main's first-parent line. Every landing moves main by exactly one new commit C, a merge commit with two parents: first parent the main the gate judged against (the task's base), second parent the worker's pushed head that was judged (the fresh head `freshness()` accepted). Always, also when main is an ancestor of the pushed head: never a fast-forward to a worker's commit. C's tree is the pushed head's tree when main is its ancestor, and otherwise the merge by main's merge rules as today (`--attr-source=<main>`; a conflict is still `conflict`). So `git log --first-parent main` is one line per landed task, and every checkpoint stays reachable from main through the second parents, off that line.
   Why a merge commit and not a squash (this is decided; do not build a squash):
   - History. The checkpoints must stay reachable. A squash keeps them only through some other ref, which needs its own push and its own recorded outcome (§14), and is not on the main that mirrors to GitHub. A merge commit keeps them through main itself, with no new ref and no new side effect.
   - The worker's branch and the freshness rule. Agent branches are never rewritten, and the pushed head must contain the latest checkpoint. After a merge landing, the worker's head is an ancestor of main, so the next merge of main into its branch (`main_merge`, at delivery) has the landing as merge base and is clean. After a squash, main never contains the worker's commits: every later merge of main into that branch starts from the old fork point and sees the same change from both sides, which conflicts as soon as the worker edited those lines again.
   - The compare-and-swap push. It is unchanged either way: C's first parent is the base, so `--force-with-lease=<main>:<base>` moves main forward by one commit, and a main that moved still sends the task back as `stale`.
   - Bisection. `git bisect start --first-parent` (git 2.29 and later) visits only landings, each one gated. A plain bisect may stop on an ungated checkpoint, which a squash would avoid. That is the price of keeping the history, and the docs say so.
   - Reverts. `git revert -m 1 <C>` undoes exactly one task. Because the worker's commits are already in main's history, a reverted objective comes back as a new task from the current main (as Spawn does anyway), or by reverting the revert. It never comes back by merging the same branch again. The docs say so.
2. The gate judges the commit that lands. C, message included, is built before the gate runs, as the candidate is now. The `task.gated` accepted record names it in `candidate`, `land()` pushes exactly that commit, and the `task.landed` record names it in `to`. A crash after the push lands the same C on the next pass, as `land()` already checks.
3. The message says what landed:
   - Its first line holds, for an objective task, the objective's title, and names the objective and the task, e.g. `Greet the harbour (objective 007, task 42)`. For a task without an objective, it holds the first non-empty line of its brief (cut to a sane length) and the task id. It is never `spawn checkpoint ...`.
   - The message names the task as `task <id>` and the objective as `objective <id>` (zero padding is fine) somewhere in it, matched case-insensitively.
   - After the first line, a blank line and a summary taken from the task's report as the record holds it, never read from a workspace: the report's `## What changed` section, or the whole report trimmed when it has no such section, at most a few thousand characters.
   - Trailers after it are welcome (`Spawn-Task: <id>`, `Spawn-Objective: <id>`, the judged head). But the summary is text a worker wrote, so it must never become a trailer: no line of the summary may make `names_files_outside_git` true for the message, or make it carry any `Spawn-` trailer the summary did not earn (indent or drop such lines). A report naming a large-file manifest must not make main unmountable.
   - The message holds no other task's id or summary. The author and committer stay `LANDING_IDENTITY`, unsigned, whatever the host's git configuration.
   - A branch head that names a large-file manifest still lands without that trailer on main, as now (C's message is the integrator's).
4. Nothing else moves. Unchanged: the freshness rule (stale pushes do not land), agent branches (the integrator never moves `refs/heads/<agent>`), the halt rules (the baseline is C, so "the source's main not where the last landing left it" holds), the gate's inputs (base and candidate, now C), the scenario count, the budget, and the review path (accept = review lands the same way). Only the integrator writes C, and no other component writes to main.
5. Say it in the module comment of integrate.rs (step 4), in docs/storage.md ("Landing"), in docs/fleet-architecture.md §10.3 and in the git contract of docs/design.md §10: the landing commit's shape, its message, `--first-parent` for log and bisect, and `revert -m 1`.
Add unit tests in integrate.rs, with a scratch mirror as the existing landing tests do:
- `landing_candidate` makes a two-parent commit with the message, both when main is an ancestor of the pushed head (tree equal to the head's) and when main moved (tree equal to the merge);
- the message of an objective task, of a task without an objective, of a report without `## What changed`, and of a very long report (bounded);
- a report holding a `Spawn-Large: <64 hex>` line does not make the message name files outside git;
- a large-file-manifest head lands with C's message.
Existing tests that assert the old shape (for example `a_conflict_verdict_leaves_markers_the_resolution_merges_main_and_lands`, whose resolved head was the candidate itself) are updated to the new shape, not deleted or ignored.

The gate judges this with rsi/scenarios/014.sh (read it). A resident `scribe` of a gated objective mission (accept = gate, one worker) runs live under a real `spawn loop` with a fake engine, no model judge and no supervisor. `spawn integrate --once` passes, run by the scenario, land its work through a recording gate that accepts every candidate. The backlog holds objectives 931 (`Greet the harbour with a kestrel`, writes HARBOUR.txt) and 932 (`Mark the lighthouse with an osprey`, writes LIGHT.txt). Each report's `## What changed` is `summary: <file> now holds <word>`, a sentence no brief contains. Once both have landed:
- (1) main's first-parent line above the base commit is exactly two commits, and the first one's first parent is the base;
- (2) each one's first line holds its objective's title and is not `spawn checkpoint ...`; its message names its task and objective, holds its report's summary after the first line, and holds neither the other task's id nor its summary;
- (3) each one's tree is the tree of the candidate in its task's `task.gated` accepted record;
- (4) each task's `task.landed` record names that commit in `to`;
- (5) every checkpoint the resident recorded before the second task was gated is reachable from main.
On 6c9eb41 it fails at (2): "the landing of task 1 reads like a checkpoint: [spawn checkpoint exec_1]". A squash (one parent) fails at (5). It exits 0 when every check passes, 1 when an assertion fails, 2 on a harness failure.

Rules: never edit the protected paths, which the gate rejects: rsi/, scripts/ (scripts/rsi/, scripts/blackbox/, scripts/e2e.sh among them), deploy/, all of web/ except web/src/ and web/index.html, rust-toolchain files and .cargo/. The gate also rejects fewer runnable tests than the base (do not delete, rename, ignore or disable tests), any lint relaxation ([lints] tables, clippy.toml, a new crate-level #![allow]/#![expect], a removed #![warn]/#![deny]) and any build-time code (build.rs, .cargo/, a `build =` key in a Cargo.toml). The gate builds offline from the cargo caches already on the host: a new crate builds only if it is already in ~/.cargo/registry. Keep every existing check green (clippy -D warnings, the workspace tests, the e2e, the black-box scenarios, the web build) and add tests of your own for the new behaviour.
